title: CDS data modeling
intro: Explain the data model before discussing annotations. A strong answer connects entity identity, association cardinality, authorization and the intended consumer. Distinguish a reusable CDS model from a transactional RAP projection and from an analytical query.

sources.title: SAP RAP: implementing sorting of virtual elements

questions.question: What does ABAP CDS add to a SQL query?
questions.answer: CDS turns a database query into a reusable ABAP data model. It can describe fields, relationships, currency meanings, annotations, and read-access rules. Several apps can use that model instead of rebuilding the same query. SQL still produces the database result. If users must create or change business objects, RAP behavior supplies those operations separately.
questions.detail:
A sales-order list needs an order number, customer, and amount. A CDS model can expose these fields, connect the customer data, and identify the amount's currency. Appropriate access control can restrict which orders the caller reads. Another application can reuse this model instead of copying all the joins and rules.

That reuse also means the exposed fields and meanings matter to callers. Changing a field's meaning can break an app even when the query still runs. And a readable order model does not automatically support creating an order. For that, define the supported business operations and their behavior rather than treating a CDS SELECT as a complete transaction implementation.
questions.pitfall: A CDS definition does not automatically implement create, update and delete operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between a classic CDS view and a CDS view entity?
questions.answer: A classic CDS view creates both a CDS entity and a separately named DDIC SQL view. A CDS view entity does not create that separate SQL-view object. For new development, prefer view entities where the target release and consumers support them. Migration needs care because existing programs may call the old SQL-view name directly.
questions.detail:
Suppose a classic view declares a SQL-view name that several reports use in SELECT statements. Replacing the CDS definition with a view entity changes more than the source syntax: those reports still expect the separately named object. Find the consumers and plan how they will use the replacement.

Check release support and the requirements of tools that consume the view before converting it. Test representative reads after changing the callers, including their fields and result identity. Do not copy AbapCatalog.sqlViewName into the view entity, because it belongs to the classic pattern. The useful interview distinction is which repository objects exist and who depends on them, rather than simply calling one syntax old and the other new.
questions.pitfall: Do not copy AbapCatalog.sqlViewName into a view entity or assume all older systems support view entities.

questions.question: Association or join and how do you select cardinality?
questions.answer: A join combines sources in the current query. An association defines a relationship that a consumer can follow, often producing a join when used. Cardinality describes how many related rows can really match the ON condition. It must match the data. Declaring a relationship to-one when several rows can match can lead to incorrect results.
questions.detail:
Order 4710 has amount 100 EUR and a status with English and German texts. Joining only on Status finds both texts, so the order appears twice and a sum can incorrectly show 200 EUR. Match Status and the requested Language. If the text source is truly unique for that pair, a to-one target cardinality may be correct. Test missing texts and unexpected duplicates too.

The order's own key is a separate issue. Declaring OrderUUID as a key does not remove rows duplicated by an incomplete join. Likewise, writing a to-one cardinality does not enforce uniqueness in the text source; the ON condition and actual target data must support it. Also measure performance where needed. An association is useful for modeling relationships, but is not automatically faster than writing a join.
questions.pitfall: Associations are not automatically faster than joins and do not enforce referential integrity.

questions.question: Association versus composition in RAP?
questions.answer: Use an association for a relationship between entities. Use a composition when a child belongs to a parent within one RAP business object, such as an order item belonging to its order. That ownership affects the object's lifecycle and modeled lock and authorization dependencies. When exposing projections, redirect these relationships to the matching projected entities.
questions.detail:
An order item has its own table row, but it normally exists as part of an order. A composition expresses that ownership and supports operations such as creating items through their parent. Review the modeled delete behavior and how children depend on the root for locking and authorization. Those choices must match the business object's lifecycle.

A customer linked to the order is different: deleting the order should not normally delete the customer. That relationship belongs as an association rather than a composition. In the app's projections, make sure navigation points to the projected order and item entities. A foreign key alone does not decide whether the target is an owned child.
questions.pitfall: Not every foreign key should become a composition; lifecycle ownership is the deciding factor.

questions.question: What do interface composite consumption and projection mean?
questions.answer: These names describe different modeling jobs. Interface views aim at reuse, and consumption views serve particular consumers. VDM basic, composite, and consumption annotations describe a modeling convention. A RAP projection exposes a supported view of one underlying entity for a use case. Its provider contract limits what it can do. None of these labels publishes a service by itself.
questions.detail:
Two apps may share the same request model but need different fields and operations. Keep common meanings in the reusable model. Give each app an appropriate projection, and redirect its relationships consistently so navigation reaches the intended projected entities. This avoids copying core business definitions for every screen.

Do not add an extra CDS layer just to satisfy a naming diagram if it adds no useful responsibility. Likewise, labeling a view composite does not make it eligible for every projection feature or create a service binding. Check the provider contract before adding joins or expressions. The key explanation is what each layer does for a consumer and what changes it protects that consumer from.
questions.pitfall: A VDM composite annotation is neither a prerequisite for service binding nor permission to perform arbitrary joins in a RAP projection.

questions.question: What are CDS abstract and custom entities?
questions.answer: An abstract entity defines a structured type, for example the input of an action. It does not produce a database query result. A custom entity defines query data that an ABAP provider supplies instead of generated SQL. Neither means an abstract ABAP superclass. Choose according to whether you need a data shape or an implemented query.
questions.detail:
A Submit action might need a comment and requested approval date. An abstract entity can describe that input shape; the action is still declared in the behavior definition. There is no table of action parameters to read merely because this type exists.

For a supplier search backed by a remote service, a custom entity can describe the result fields while an ABAP query provider fetches the data. That provider must respect the requested filters, ordering, paging, count, and permissions as applicable. Returning the remote service's first page without honoring the caller's request can make the list misleading. The custom entity supplies the model, not an automatic implementation of those query rules.
questions.pitfall: Do not describe an abstract entity as a BO that other CDS entities inherit and persist.

questions.question: Does DCL on a base view automatically protect every higher view?
questions.answer: No. Access control on a lower CDS view does not automatically protect every view built on it. Design the read rules for the entity that callers actually access. Supported DCL inheritance can reuse conditions with the required mappings. The #CHECK annotation alone creates no rule. RAP permissions for changing objects are a separate check.
questions.detail:
Assume the base order model restricts Lea to sales organization A, and a service exposes a higher consumption view. Test that exposed view through its actual read path. If order B1 from organization B appears alongside A1, the protected base view has not proved the service is protected. Check the customer value help separately so it does not reveal B-Customer either.

Inspect the effective DCL on the accessed entity and any inherited conditions and field mappings. Include users with different permissions and realistic filters in the test. Then test update or approval permission separately in RAP. A correct read filter limits visible rows; it does not automatically decide whether the user may execute every action on those rows.
questions.pitfall: DCL on one layer does not automatically secure an arbitrary view-on-view stack.

questions.question: Where do UI annotations and value helps belong?
questions.answer: Put supported UI and value-help annotations in metadata extensions when the model allows it. Keep data meanings, such as the link between an amount and its currency, in the data model. Check which annotations and extension layers the release supports. A value help makes input easier, but the backend must still check submitted values and permissions.
questions.detail:
A Fiori elements list shows a request amount and offers a cost-center value help. A metadata extension can describe the list columns and the supported value-help setup. The CDS data model still needs to say which currency belongs to the amount so consumers interpret the value correctly.

Now call the service directly and submit a cost center that the value help would never offer. The backend must reject it when it violates a business rule or permission. Hiding a field or narrowing a picker is not enough. Also check annotation layer precedence: a customer or partner extension may interact with existing metadata, so moving every annotation mechanically can change the resulting UI.
questions.pitfall: UI.hidden and a value help are not security or data-integrity controls.

questions.question: What is a virtual element and what are its limits?
questions.answer: A virtual element is calculated in ABAP for a supported query scenario, often through a SADL calculation exit. It is not a stored database column. That matters when callers want to filter or sort by it. Those operations need explicit supported handling, and support varies by service and release. Use database-side modeling when efficient database filtering is essential.
questions.detail:
A list might display a status description calculated from data that is not stored in its main table. A virtual element can be suitable if the supported query flow calls the calculation and supplies the needed input fields. Request only the inputs required rather than fetching unrelated data for every row.

Now suppose users need to sort thousands of rows by that value before paging. A calculation performed after reading a page cannot automatically produce the correct global order. Check supported sorting or filtering handling, or choose a different model. A UI requestAtLeast hint can help a particular UI request fields, but it is not a guarantee for every possible consumer.
questions.pitfall: requestAtLeast is a UI request hint, not a universal guarantee that every consumer calculates a virtual element.

questions.question: How do analytical CDS models differ from transactional models?
questions.answer: An analytical model answers questions such as totals by month or company. It organizes measures, dimensions, and supported aggregation rules. A transactional RAP model identifies individual objects and exposes operations such as Create or Approve. A model designed for one job is not automatically correct for the other. Always account for currencies, units, and the actual query engine.
questions.detail:
An order app may display individual orders and allow approval. A spending report instead groups values by supplier and month. If some orders are in EUR and others in USD, adding the raw amounts gives a number without a valid common currency. Group them appropriately or use the intended conversion before interpreting a total.

Check what the selected analytical engine, service protocol, and client actually support. A cube or analytical query has responsibilities that an ordinary transactional list does not. Merely adding a VDM annotation or sending $apply does not prove that grouping, conversion, and aggregation have the intended meaning. Test a small dataset with known mixed currencies before trusting the totals.
questions.pitfall: A VDM annotation or an OData $apply request alone does not guarantee correct analytical semantics.

questions.question: How do CDS keys and database keys relate?
questions.answer: A CDS key tells consumers which fields identify a row. It does not force the query result to be unique. A database key enforces uniqueness in a table, but joins and grouping can change the result. RAP and OData need a stable, truly unique identity. Check the complete result, not just the key declarations.
questions.detail:
Imagine flight rows identified by carrier, connection, and flight date. If a CDS entity marks only carrier and connection as keys, two flights on different dates appear to have the same identity to the client. A list may confuse them or address the wrong row even though the database has two valid records.

Include the fields needed to identify one result row and check what joins do to that uniqueness. Joining a flight to several related rows can multiply the result again. Marking another field as key does not remove duplicates or repair the underlying query. Test with realistic repeated business values, not just sample data where every connection happens to appear once.
questions.pitfall: Marking an element key does not remove duplicate rows.

questions.question: Is a maintenance view a RAP view and how are defaults supplied?
questions.answer: A classic maintenance view belongs to DDIC table or view maintenance, often used through SM30. A RAP app uses a CDS model and behavior to provide a different kind of maintenance application. In RAP, determinations or supported defaulting functions can supply defaults. The chosen UI and metadata control presentation. First clarify which maintenance approach the question means.
questions.detail:
A team asks for a small configuration maintenance screen. If it means an existing SM30 dialog, examine its maintenance events and supported classic setup. If it means a Fiori RAP app, design the CDS entities and behavior, including who may change entries and how default values are supplied. The word maintenance does not make these the same technology.

For example, a RAP determination may fill an initial currency while backend checks still reject invalid input. UI annotations can help present the fields, but they do not replace that behavior. Do not invent generic Metadata.ignore or Metadata.defaultValue annotations as a shortcut: verify the actual supported defaulting and visibility mechanisms for the chosen app.
questions.pitfall: Metadata.ignore and Metadata.defaultValue are not generic annotations that implement maintenance behavior.
